food.text: Catherine of Braganza brought the Portuguese habit of tea to England around 1660. At first its expense restricted it to wealthy consumers, but the price gradually dropped until, by the 19th century, its use was widespread.

In the second half of the sixteenth century, almost half the years in Scotland saw local or national scarcity of food, following frequent harvest failures. Large quantities of grain had to be shipped in from the Baltic, which was referred to as Scotland's "emergency granary". The hardship was made worse by outbreaks of plague, with major epidemics in 1584–88 and 1597–1609.
food.source_title: Economy of Scotland in the early modern period

food.text: Under Louis XIV, much of the French countryside remained poor and overpopulated. According to some monarchist apologists, peasants' resistance to the potato and other new agricultural innovations, and their continued reliance on cereal crops, led to repeated catastrophic famines long after they had ceased in the rest of Western Europe. Famine in 1692–1693 killed up to two million people, and between 1693 and 1694 France lost 6% of its population. In the extremely harsh winter of 1709, France lost 3.5% of its population.
food.source_title: France in the early modern period

food.text: Printed cookery books arrived gradually in early modern England, but the first, the printer Richard Pynson's 1500 Boke of Cokery, was compiled from medieval texts. The number of titles then expanded rapidly towards the end of the century.
Coffee was introduced to England in the 16th century and became popular by the 17th, especially in coffee houses. The first coffee house opened in Oxford in 1650.

Late sixteenth-century English cookery books were of two kinds. Some collected "secrets" on confectionery and health remedies for aristocratic ladies, while others gave advice on cookery and household management for women from more ordinary backgrounds. Thomas Dawson's The Good Huswifes Jewell appeared in 1585.
Curry was introduced from the Indian subcontinent and adapted to English tastes from the eighteenth century. An early example is Hannah Glasse's recipe for chicken "currey".

Chocolate arrived in England from France around 1657, around the same time as tea and coffee, and met an initial backlash from those with medical concerns. Cocoa was supplied by Jamaican plantations after the British conquered the Spanish territory in 1655. By the end of the 17th century it was compulsory to include chocolate in British Navy rations.

Hannah Glasse's 1747 book The Art of Cookery Made Plain and Easy included a recipe titled "To make a Currey the Indian Way". Clarissa Dickson-Wright later observed that its spices did not resemble those of a modern curry, but that the dish had a good flavour.
tags: The Art of Cookery Made Plain and Easy

food.text: Hot chocolate was a popular drink in England by the 17th century, long before chocolate was used as a food. Like tea and coffee, it came from outside Europe.
Scotland's grain trade with the Baltic ran mainly through Danzig in Poland, and later through Königsberg and Riga. It was so important that Scottish colonies were established in these ports.
food.source_title: Economy of Scotland in the early modern period

food.text: Greenock enlarged its port in 1710 and sent its first ship to the Americas in 1719. It was soon playing a major part in importing sugar and rum into Scotland.
food.source_title: Economy of Scotland in the early modern period

food.text: A "Spanish Sauce" for pheasant appears in Vincent La Chapelle's 1733 cookery book Le Cuisinier moderne. His recipe calls for onions, carrots, gravy, ham essence, lemon, garlic, basil, thyme, bay leaf, parsley, green onion and white wine, and optionally partridges.

In the late 18th century, many British women created handwritten cookbooks that included Indian-style dishes. These household collections helped carry the flavours of Anglo-Indian cooking into British kitchens.

One tale says Anne of Austria brought Spanish cooks to the French court, who added tomatoes to the brown sauce. A similar story credits the Spanish cooks of Louis XIV's wife, Maria Theresa of Spain. There is no record of Spanish cooks in the court's kitchens, so these explanations appear baseless.

art.text: In the 17th century Paris was the largest city in Europe, with half a million people, matched in size only by London. Its monarchs oversaw the building of the Pont Neuf, the Palais Royal, the Place des Vosges and the Luxembourg Garden. The city also became home to the new Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture.
tags: Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture

art.text: Art of the English Renaissance showed a strong interest in portraiture, and the portrait miniature was more popular in England than anywhere else. Sculpture of the time was mainly architectural or made for monumental tombs.

In the later 17th century, Baroque architecture, a version of Classicism marked by heavy massing and ostentatiously elaborate decoration, became widespread in England. Grand Baroque country houses began to appear in the 1690s, with Chatsworth House and Castle Howard as leading examples.

From the 16th century, the Renaissance made Italy the main source of stylistic developments in European art. That changed late in the reign of Louis XIV, when France became the leading artistic influence, especially during the Rococo and Neoclassicism periods.

The English Reformation was antipathetic to art. It brought England's strong national tradition of religious painting to an abrupt stop and led to the destruction of almost all wall-paintings, so only illuminated manuscripts now survive in good numbers.

The artists of the Tudor court and their successors until the early 18th century included influential imported talents such as Hans Holbein the Younger, Anthony van Dyck and Peter Paul Rubens. Sir Peter Lely became a naturalised English subject in 1662, and Sir Godfrey Kneller was naturalised by the time of his 1691 knighthood.

The most significant English Baroque architects after Wren were Sir John Vanbrugh and Nicholas Hawksmoor. They adapted the Baroque style to English tastes in houses such as Blenheim Palace, Seaton Delaval Hall and Easton Neston.
Guillaume Coustou the Elder was famous for his last royal commission, the Marly Horses (1743–1745). Robert Le Lorrain was celebrated for his Sun Horses relief in the Hôtel de Rohan in Paris (1737).

Jean-Baptiste Pigalle was celebrated for his impressive funerary monument of Maurice de Saxe in Strasbourg, made between 1753 and 1765. In 1776 he also produced a naked statue of Voltaire portrayed as an antique philosopher.

Samuel Cooper (1609–1672) was an accomplished miniaturist in Hilliard's tradition. So was his brother Alexander Cooper, and their uncle John Hoskins was another notable portrait miniaturist of the period.

Jean-Antoine Houdon was noted for his busts of celebrated authors and statesmen. His bronzes with clean lines, like his allegory of Winter, combined the elongation of the body reminiscent of Mannerism with the colder rigor of Neoclassicism.

war.text: The English Civil War was a series of wars between Royalists and Parliamentarians in the Kingdom of England from 1642 to 1651. The first war was fought mainly over the balance of power between Parliament and Charles I. It ended in June 1646 with a Royalist defeat and the king in custody.

After the Stuarts lost the throne when James II fled to France in 1688, the Jacobites kept up the Stuart claim. He and his son James Francis Edward Stuart claimed to be the legitimate kings, backed by Louis XIV. The Jacobites plotted seaborne invasions, with major attempts in the risings of 1715 and 1745, but both failed to rally significant popular support.

France allied with its traditional Habsburg enemy in the "Diplomatic Revolution" of 1756, against the rising power of Britain and Prussia. The alliance led to costly failure in the Seven Years' War (1756 to 1763). France lost its North American colonies as a result.
war.source_title: France in the early modern period

war.text: Royalist defeat in the Second English Civil War of 1648 ended with Charles I beheaded on a scaffold in front of the Banqueting House of the Palace of Whitehall on 30 January 1649. Most Parliamentarians had gone to war in 1642 to assert Parliament's right to take part in government, not to abolish the monarchy. The Commonwealth of England was then established.

The third civil war, from 1649 to 1651, saw fighting between supporters of King Charles II and supporters of the Rump Parliament. The whole Civil War ended with the Parliamentary victory at the Battle of Worcester on 3 September 1651.

Oliver Cromwell ruled the Protectorate as Lord Protector, effectively a military dictator, until his death in 1658. His rule fell between two periods of republican Commonwealth government, which ruled from 1649 to 1653 and from 1659 to 1660.

Louis XIV's wars brought territorial gains. The War of Devolution (1667 to 1668) and the Franco-Dutch War (1672 to 1678) won Artois, western Flanders and the free county of Burgundy. The cost was the increasingly concerted opposition of rival powers.
war.source_title: France in the early modern period

war.text: In 1649 joint Royalist and Confederate forces under James Butler, Duke of Ormonde besieged the Parliamentary army in Dublin but were routed at the Battle of Rathmines on 2 August. Admiral Robert Blake had blockaded Prince Rupert's fleet in Kinsale, and Oliver Cromwell landed at Dublin on 15 August 1649 with an army. After the Siege of Drogheda, nearly 3,500 people were massacred, around 2,700 Royalist soldiers and 700 others, including civilians, prisoners and Catholic priests, all of whom Cromwell claimed had carried arms. The Irish still remember it.

Concern over the political influence of radicals within the New Model Army, like Oliver Cromwell, led to an unlikely alliance. Moderate Parliamentarians joined the Royalists, supported by the Covenanter Scots. Royalist defeat in the Second English Civil War followed in 1648.

Ireland had been at war continually since the rebellion of 1641, and the Irish Confederates controlled most of the island. Threatened by the armies of the English Parliament after Charles I's arrest in 1648, they signed a treaty of alliance with the English Royalists.

The Jacobite defeat at the Battle of Culloden in 1746 ended any realistic hope of a Stuart restoration. The throne had passed to the Protestant House of Hanover, starting with George I in 1714. Historian Basil Williams concludes, "there was never any serious danger to the dynasty."

Many officers and veteran soldiers in the English Civil War had fought in European wars. These included the Eighty Years' War between the Spanish and the Dutch, which began in 1568, and earlier phases of the Thirty Years' War, which began in 1618 and concluded in 1648.

Count de Brègy recruited soldiers in Poland for the French army in 1646–1648, and about 3,000 travelled via Gdańsk to Flanders to fight around Dunkirk. A French historian says they were commanded by one "Sirot", whom some historians identify as the Cossack Ivan Sirko.

literature.text: Alexander Pope's Rape of the Lock (1712–1717) and The Dunciad (1728–1743) are still considered to be the greatest mock-heroic poems ever written. Pope also translated the Iliad (1715–1720) and the Odyssey (1725–1726). Since his death, he has been in a constant state of re-evaluation.

In the 1690s, the fairy tale began to appear in French literature. The best-known collection of traditional tales, liberally adapted, was by Charles Perrault in 1697. Many others were published too, including those by Henriette-Julie de Murat and Madame d'Aulnoy.

The Reformation's call to let people interpret the Bible for themselves helped launch a vernacular English literature. William Tyndale published his own translation in 1526, and the Geneva Bible followed in 1560. These would be predecessors to the King James Version.

Antoine Galland produced the first French, and indeed the first modern, translation of the Thousand and One Nights in 1704, with another translation appearing in 1710–12. A major revolution followed, as it influenced the 18th-century short stories of Voltaire, Diderot and many others.

Oliver Goldsmith wrote The Vicar of Wakefield (1766), the pastoral poem The Deserted Village (1770) and two plays, including She Stoops to Conquer (1773). Both he and Richard Brinsley Sheridan reacted against the sentimental comedy of 18th-century theatre. They wrote plays closer to the style of Restoration comedy.

Devotional books were the best sellers of all literary works in 17th-century France, amid the religious fervor unleashed by the Counter-Reformation. Yet some writers, such as Théophile de Viau and Charles de Saint-Evremond, were considered "libertine". Inspired by Epicurus and the publication of Petronius, they professed doubts of religious or moral matters.

William Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra was first performed in 1608. It was largely based on Plutarch and gave a somewhat salacious view of Cleopatra, in stark contrast to England's own Virgin Queen.

Cervantes' Exemplary Tales appeared in French beginning in 1614, and Don Quixote followed in French translation in 1614–1618. Together with the Spanish picaresque novel such as Lazarillo de Tormes, they influenced French novelists to describe and satirize their own era and its excesses.

Richard Brinsley Sheridan's first play, The Rivals (1775), was performed at Covent Garden and was an instant success. He went on to become the most significant London playwright of the late 18th century, with a play like The School for Scandal.

Sir Francis Bacon's utopian narrative New Atlantis was published in Latin as Nova Atlantis in 1624 and in English in 1627. Thomas More's Utopia (1516) was likewise written in Latin, showing that English writers of the era still often worked in that language.

Commedia dell'arte performers improvised in the streets of Italy and France from the 16th to the 18th century, and some of their plays were written down. Both the written plays and the improvisation influenced literature of the time, particularly the work of Molière.
In Renaissance literature, new genres such as the essay, associated with Montaigne, appeared. So did new metrical forms such as the Spenserian stanza, named for the poet Edmund Spenser.

Queen Elizabeth I of England died in 1603, and alleged letters of Cleopatra were published in German in 1606. Together these inspired Samuel Daniel to alter and republish his 1594 play Cleopatra in 1607.

science.text: The development of lead glass in the late 17th century propelled England to the forefront of the glass industry. It also paved the way for advancements in the Industrial Revolution.

Isaac Newton's Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687) dissolved the ancient boundary between the celestial and the terrestrial. It showed that a single mathematical law, the law of universal gravitation, ruled both realms, and it was the first great unification of physics.

Paris in the 17th century was a flourishing center of French science. It saw the founding of the Paris Observatory, the French Academy of Sciences and the first botanical garden in Paris, which also became the first park in Paris open to the public.

Paris in the 17th century, a city of half a million people, saw a run of urban innovations. They included the first street lighting, the first public transport, the first building code, and the first new aqueduct since the Roman era.

From 1581 to 1584, Parliament grew worried about the country's wood supply. Many high-temperature industries depended on wood for fuel, and this was diminishing the forests. The original decree prohibited wood fuel unless it came from one's own land.

English coffeehouses of the 17th and 18th centuries hosted debates on philosophy and the natural sciences, alongside politics and gossip. Historians associate them with the Age of Enlightenment, describing them as an alternate sphere supplementary to the university.
science.source_title: English coffeehouses in the 17th and 18th centuries

science.text: In 1631 Pierre Gassendi tracked the transit of Mercury across the Sun, using Kepler's Rudolphine Tables for his predictions. He projected an image from a telescope onto a screen, and Richard Popkin says he was one of the first to formulate the modern scientific outlook.

English glassmaking was reshaped by immigrants from Europe, who brought changes in furnace technology and raw materials and created a better quality glass. Production also evolved from small family-run glass houses to large monopolies granted by the Crown.
By 1609, Sir Edward Zouche was granted a patent to experiment with coal as the main fuel for a furnace at Winchester. By 1615 Parliament had banned the use of wood fuel.

The Weald was becoming deforested by the early 17th century. Glassmaking spread to where timber was available to fire furnaces, including Hampshire, Gloucestershire, North Staffordshire and the Scottish Borders.

A glasshouse recovered at Bagot's Park, Staffordshire, dates from circa 1535 and held an early melting furnace and a smaller annealing furnace. The melting furnace had a central flue cut into the floor to create a draught, letting it reach 1200 °C to melt the glass.

Until the mid-17th century, coffee was consumed mainly for its supposed medicinal properties, and experiments with it led to supposed cures for ailments such as "head-melancholy", gout, scurvy, smallpox and excessive drunkenness. Some people feared it did more harm than good, and that heavy drinking could cause languor, paralysis, heart conditions, trembling limbs and nervous disorders. Oxford, with its exotic scholarship interests and energetic experimental community, was a ripe place to serve it socially, and the first English coffeehouse opened there in 1650 at the Angel coaching inn.
science.source_title: English coffeehouses in the 17th and 18th centuries

science.text: At Bagot's Park, cullet heaps of broken glass were found on either side of the furnace, suggesting a flux was used to reduce melting temperatures. Crushed white pebbles at the bottom of pots may reflect the silica source used at the site.

politics.text: Louis XIV reigned from 1643 to 1715, one of the longest reigns in history. He eliminated the remnants of medieval feudalism and built a centralized state under an absolute monarch. That system lasted until the French Revolution and beyond.
politics.source_title: France in the early modern period

politics.text: The Glorious Revolution began in 1688 with the Dutch Republic invading England. Afterward, England became a constitutional monarchy. The article notes that English monarchs had grown increasingly involved in conflicts with Parliament through the century.

The English Civil War ran from 1642 to 1651 between Parliamentarians, known as Roundheads, and Royalists, known as Cavaliers. It led to the trial and execution of King Charles I, who was put to death in 1649, and to the exile of his son Charles II. It ended with the Parliamentary victory at the Battle of Worcester on 3 September 1651. After it came the Interregnum, a period from 1651 to 1660 when England had no king.

Louis XIV turned the Palace of Versailles from a hunting lodge into what the article calls a gilded prison. A greatly expanded royal court could be kept under surveillance there, which weakened and subjugated the semi-feudal French nobility to absolute monarchy.

In 1688 King James II fled to France, and the House of Stuart lost the throne. He and his son James Francis Edward Stuart still claimed to be the legitimate kings, backed by Louis XIV. The throne passed to the Protestant House of Hanover, starting with George I in 1714.

The Diggers were founded by Gerrard Winstanley in 1649. They tried to reform the social order by creating small egalitarian rural communities based on agrarian life. They were one of several nonconformist dissenting groups that emerged at the time.

The Jacobites plotted seaborne invasions of Britain, with major attempts in 1715 and 1745. Neither rallied significant popular support. The Jacobite defeat at the Battle of Culloden in 1746 ended any realistic hope of a Stuart restoration.

The Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659 formalised France's seizure of Roussillon from Spain in 1642. It followed the crushing of the ephemeral Catalan Republic. The treaty also ushered in a short period of peace after the Franco-Spanish War.

The French tricolour flag was approved by the Constituent Assembly on 24 October 1790. On 15 February 1794 the order was reversed to blue-white-red, the current design. The flag combines royalist white with republican red, and came to be seen as a symbol of moderation.

philosophy.text: In 1637 René Descartes developed his famous proposition Cogito, ergo sum. Early 17th-century philosophy is often called the Age of Rationalism, coming after Renaissance philosophy and before the Enlightenment.

Enlightenment philosophy originated in France and aimed for the triumph of reason over faith and belief. Its thinkers opposed religious and political persecution, and their works influenced the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen.
tags: Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen

philosophy.text: In seventeenth-century England, coffeehouses became places where people debated philosophy and the natural sciences, along with politics and gossip. Historians often link them to the Age of Enlightenment, calling them an alternate sphere supplementary to the university.
philosophy.source_title: English coffeehouses in the 17th and 18th centuries

philosophy.text: Because they criticised the established order, Enlightenment philosophers were chased by the authorities and had to resort to subterfuge to escape prison. François-Marie Arouet took the pseudonym Voltaire, and Montesquieu published his Persian Letters anonymously in Holland in 1721.
Pierre Charron, a follower of Montaigne, wrote On Wisdom in 1601. It argued that ethics could be separated from religion, and that one attacks reason to boost faith and wisdom.
Antoine Arnauld and Pierre Nicole produced the Port-Royal Logic in 1662. It was described as the most influential logic book after Aristotle and before the end of the nineteenth century.

Diderot's Letter on the Blind for the Use of those who can See landed him in prison at the Château de Vincennes. Voltaire was accused of writing pamphlets criticising Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, and was imprisoned in the Bastille.

Bossuet supported the 1685 revocation of the Edict of Nantes, which abolished the rights of the Protestant minority. He also banned the work of the Oratorian Richard Simon, who had been influenced by the Pre-Adamite theorist Isaac La Peyrère.

culture.text: Paris in the 17th century was the largest city in Europe, with a population of half a million, matched in size only by London. It saw the building of the Pont Neuf, the Place des Vosges and the Luxembourg Garden, and the founding of the Comédie-Française.

Under Louis XIV, his minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert brought French luxury industries such as textile and porcelain under royal control. The architecture, furniture, fashion and etiquette of the court at the Château de Versailles became the preeminent model of noble culture in France and, to a great degree, throughout Europe.

About 30% of the French population converted to Protestantism in the 16th century and became known as Huguenots. The national monarchy felt threatened by people who wanted to leave the established state religion, and Protestants were discriminated against and suppressed. On 24 August 1572 the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre took place in Paris, and the French Wars of Religion are considered to have begun, a civil war between Catholics led by Henry I, Duke of Guise and Protestants led by Henri de Navarre.

In early modern Scotland, an estimated 4,000 to 6,000 people were tried for witchcraft, a much higher rate than in neighbouring England. Seventy-five per cent of the accused were women, and modern estimates indicate that more than 1,500 people were executed. Most were strangled at the stake and then had their bodies burned, though in some cases the convicted were burned alive.
culture.source_title: Witch trials in early modern Scotland

culture.text: Fireworks were first mentioned in Paris in 1581. The first large display was given on April 12, 1612, following the Carrousel that marked the opening of the place Royale and the proposed marriage of Louis XIII with Anne of Austria.

In 1681 Louis XIV began the persecution of Huguenots by introducing the dragonnades, a wave of violence that intimidated Protestants into converting to Catholicism. He made the policy official with the 1685 revocation of the Edict of Nantes. Estimates range from 200,000 to 500,000 Protestants who fled France over the following two decades, seeking asylum in places such as England, the United Provinces and Denmark.

King James VI took a major part in the North Berwick witch trials, which began in 1590, as both a "victim" and an investigator. He set up royal commissions to hunt down witches, recommended torture in dealing with suspects, and is known to have personally supervised the torture of women accused of being witches. He published a defence of witch-hunting in the Daemonologie in 1597, but appears to have become increasingly sceptical and eventually took steps to limit prosecutions.
culture.source_title: Witch trials in early modern Scotland

culture.text: Under Richelieu, minister to Louis XIII, the independent Académie française came under state supervision. It became an official organ of control over the French language and seventeenth-century literature.

In 1618 a fireworks show over the Seine was more spectacular, with rockets that, according to the Abbot of Marolles, "burst into stars and serpents of fire." All fireworks in Paris were white or pale gold until colored fireworks arrived from China in the 18th century.

The Paris of the 17th century also saw urban firsts: the first street lighting, the first public transport, the first building code, and the first new aqueduct since the Roman era. Its first botanical garden also became the first park in Paris open to the public.

In 1615 Paris fireworks introduced allegorical figures of Jupiter on an eagle and Hercules, representing the King. They were made of fireworks mounted on scaffolds next to the Seine and on a balcony of the Louvre.
